entry.title: Translating ESBMC programs into Lean: what a second prover adds

link.title: Translating ESBMC programs into Lean: what a second prover adds

entry.content:
A model checker reports one of three verdicts: safe, unsafe or unknown. ESBMC prints them as VERIFICATION SUCCESSFUL, VERIFICATION FAILED and VERIFICATION UNKNOWN. An unsafe verdict is easy to validate, because it comes with a counterexample that can be replayed against the program. A safe verdict is harder. It is the output of a parser, a symbolic execution engine, a simplifier, an SMT encoding and a solver working in sequence, and a defect in any of them can make an incorrect program look safe. Our last post ended by asking who checks the checker. One way to answer is to give the same program to a second prover that works differently and see whether the two agree.

ESBMC is the SMT-based model checker that we develop [1]. Its front ends for C, C++, Python, Solidity and ladder diagrams all produce the same intermediate language, the GOTO program. A new option, --goto2lean, prints that program as Lean 4 definitions, together with a theorem stating that no assertion fails. Lean is a proof assistant: a proof counts only once Lean’s kernel, a small checker, has accepted it. So far the translator handles Booleans and integers, if/else, loops (one at a time), calls to non-recursive functions, and quantifiers in assertions. It rejects arrays and pointers.

The two provers can work together in more than one way. When ESBMC cannot finish a proof, Lean sometimes can, and Lean’s proof then shows which reasoning steps ESBMC was missing; we wrote some of those steps back into the C program and ESBMC finished. If the two disagree on a program, at least one of them has a bug, which is the check our last post asked for. We show both, the second with a real ESBMC bug.

flowchart LR
    S["Source<br/>C, C++ or Python"] --> G["GOTO program<br/>ESBMC front end"]
    G --> E{"ESBMC<br/>symbolic execution,<br/>SMT solver"}
    G --> T["--goto2lean<br/>weakest precondition<br/>in Lean 4"]
    T --> L{"Lean 4<br/>bv_decide, omega, grind<br/>or a supplied proof"}
    E --> V1["Verdict<br/>and counterexample"]
    L --> V2["Theorem proved<br/>or refuted"]
    V1 --> C["Compare"]
    V2 --> C

Figure 1. Two routes from the same GOTO program. Both start after the front end, so a front-end bug is invisible to both.

Note that all results below were measured on a laptop, with ESBMC’s development version and Lean 4.35.0.

A loop that ESBMC cannot finish

Our first example is a loop that adds up the first n cubes and the first n whole numbers, then asserts Nicomachus’s theorem: the sum of the cubes equals the square of the sum. For n = 4, 0 + 1 + 8 + 27 = 36 = (0 + 1 + 2 + 3)2.

unsigned nondet_uint(void);
int main(void) {
  unsigned n = nondet_uint();
  unsigned s = 0, c = 0, i = 0;
  while (i < n) {
    s = s + i;
    c = c + i * i * i;
    i = i + 1;
  }
  __ESBMC_assert(c == s * s, "Nicomachus");
  return 0;
}

The program uses 32-bit unsigned arithmetic, so large values wrap around. Nicomachus’s theorem survives that. It is an equation built from additions and multiplications, both sides wrap in the same way, and the assertion holds for every n.

Proving something about a loop for every n needs a loop invariant: a fact that is true before the loop and stays true after each iteration. ESBMC does not find one here by itself, and plain k-induction answers VERIFICATION UNKNOWN. So we supplied one with __ESBMC_loop_invariant: 2 * s == i * (i - 1), c == s * s and i <= n. The hard part is the middle fact. ESBMC has to show that if c equals s * s before an iteration, then c + i * i * i equals (s + i) * (s + i) after it. It passes that question to an SMT solver, which handles 32-bit arithmetic by turning every multiplication into a circuit of logic gates and searching the circuit for a counterexample. Cubing a 32-bit number gives a large circuit. Neither of the two solvers we tried, Z3 and Bitwuzla, answered within five minutes.

esbmc ucubes.c --goto2lean produces this Lean file instead:

def main_loop1 (n : BitVec 32) (s : BitVec 32) (c : BitVec 32) (i : BitVec 32)
    (post : BitVec 32 → BitVec 32 → BitVec 32 → BitVec 32 → Prop)
    (ret : BitVec 32 → Prop) : Prop :=
  (¬(i < n) →
    post n s c i) ∧
  ((i < n) →
  let s := (s + i);
  let c := (c + ((i * i) * i));
  let i := (i + (1#32));
  main_loop1 n s c i post ret)
coinductive_fixpoint

def main (post : BitVec 32 → Prop) : Prop :=
  ∀ n : BitVec 32,
  let s := (0#32);
  let c := (0#32);
  let i := (0#32);
  main_loop1 n s c i (fun (n : BitVec 32) (s : BitVec 32) (c : BitVec 32) (i : BitVec 32) =>
    -- Nicomachus
    (c = (s * s)) ∧ (
    post (0#32))) post

theorem main_safe : Prog.main (fun _ => True) := by
  -- Not closed automatically: each loop needs an invariant (apply Prog.<loop>.coinduct).
  sorry

Listing 1. The Lean that --goto2lean generates for the loop, with the namespace and one renaming line removed. sorry is Lean’s placeholder for a missing proof.

Listing 1 is the inductive version of the program. The while loop is gone; in its place is main_loop1, a definition that refers to itself. Read it as a statement about one visit to the loop head with the current values of n, s, c and i. If i < n is false, the loop exits and the final check c = s * s must hold. Otherwise the body runs once, giving new values of s, c and i, and the same statement must hold again for those values, which is the self-reference. main makes the first visit, with s, c and i at zero and n arbitrary (the ∀). The rest of the file follows one pattern: a nondeterministic value becomes ∀, an __ESBMC_assume becomes →, and an assertion becomes ∧. One keyword is new: coinductive_fixpoint allows the loop to run forever. A run that never exits never reaches the assertion, so the theorem only constrains runs that terminate.

From that definition Lean derives a proof rule, Prog.main_loop1.coinduct. To use it, you give a property of the loop variables. You then show that it holds at the first visit, and that whenever it holds at the loop head, the statement above holds with the property in place of the self-reference. That property is the loop invariant, and the rule is the loop-invariant rule of Hoare logic. Lean derives it from the definition, so the rule itself does not have to be trusted. Replacing sorry with the invariant we gave ESBMC completes the proof:

theorem main_safe : Prog.main (fun _ => True) := by
  simp only [Prog.main]
  intro n
  apply Prog.main_loop1.coinduct n _ _
    (fun s c i => 2#32 * s = i * (i - 1#32) ∧ c = s * s ∧ i ≤ n)
  · intro s c i ⟨hs, hc, hle⟩
    refine ⟨fun hlt => ⟨?_, trivial⟩, fun hlt => ⟨?_, ?_, ?_⟩⟩
    · have : i = n := by bv_omega
      subst this; exact hc
    · grind
    · grind
    · bv_omega
  · exact ⟨by decide, by decide, by bv_omega⟩

Listing 2. The proof that replaces sorry. Lean checks it in 4.2 seconds.

After the apply ... coinduct line, Lean asks for three things: the invariant holds before the loop, it survives one iteration, and on exit it implies the assertion. Most of the remaining lines are bookkeeping, and the two grind lines do the real work. grind is Lean’s general-purpose automation, the hammer you try before writing a proof by hand. Part of what it does is algebra: it expands (s + i) * (s + i), uses 2 * s = i * (i - 1) to rewrite the result, and finds that both sides are the same polynomial, as you would on paper. It never builds a circuit, so the cube costs it no more than a sum. The gain comes from the algebra, not from Lean as such. When we replaced grind with bv_decide, the Lean tactic that does build a circuit and call a SAT solver, it timed out too.

What ESBMC can learn from Lean’s proof

Lean finished the proof, but ESBMC is the tool people run on their code, so we asked what Lean’s proof could teach it. Listing 2 does three things that ESBMC’s single query to the solver does not. It works on the start, the step and the exit as separate goals. At the exit it derives i = n from i ≤ n and ¬(i < n) and substitutes it (the have ... subst line). And grind uses the invariant’s equations as rewrite rules on the step. We tested each move by writing it back into the C program, and we also asked whether ESBMC could have supplied the invariant.

Invariants. ESBMC has an option, --synthesise-loop-invariants, that proposes invariants for loops whose counters and accumulators grow by a constant. On the counting loop from our demo (s and i both go up by one, and the program asserts s == n after the loop), it proposed (i < n || i == n || i == 0) && (0 < n || i == 0) && s == i. We pasted that predicate into the generated Lean file unchanged, and bv_decide proved the theorem in 9.5 seconds. On the Gauss and Nicomachus loops, the option reports that no loop matched its shape, because those accumulators grow by i and by i * i * i. So ESBMC can hand Lean the invariants of simple loops today. Polynomial invariants such as 2 * s == i * (i - 1) still have to come from a person or a model.

Hints. Next we copied grind’s algebra into the loop body, as four __ESBMC_assume statements: the expansion of (s + i) * (s + i), the regrouping of 2 * s * i, the substitution of i * (i - 1) for 2 * s, and the expansion of i * (i - 1) * i + i * i. Each holds for every 32-bit value. ESBMC proves the two expansions and the regrouping in under a second each, as separate programs. The substitution is congruence: equal values multiplied by the same i stay equal. The hints alone changed nothing, and neither solver answered in 300 seconds.

Separate goals. What made the difference was checking the claims one at a time. ESBMC normally sends all of a program’s claims to the solver as one query; --multi-property sends each on its own, which is what Lean’s refine does when it splits the proof into goals. With the hints and --multi-property, Z3 proves the 32-bit Nicomachus program in 6.0 seconds:

unsigned nondet_uint(void);
int main(void) {
  unsigned n = nondet_uint();
  unsigned s = 0, c = 0, i = 0;
  __ESBMC_loop_invariant(2 * s == i * (i - 1) && c == s * s && i <= n);
  while (i < n) {
    __ESBMC_assume((s + i) * (s + i) == s * s + 2 * s * i + i * i);
    __ESBMC_assume(2 * s * i == (2 * s) * i);
    __ESBMC_assume(2 * s != i * (i - 1) || (2 * s) * i == (i * (i - 1)) * i);
    __ESBMC_assume(i * (i - 1) * i + i * i == i * i * i);
    s = s + i;
    c = c + i * i * i;
    i = i + 1;
  }
  __ESBMC_assert(c == s * s, "Nicomachus");
  return 0;
}

Listing 3. The 32-bit Nicomachus program with grind’s steps written in. esbmc --loop-invariant-check --multi-property --z3 reports VERIFICATION SUCCESSFUL in 6.0 seconds.

Neither change is enough alone. Without the hints, --multi-property still times out, and so do the hints without it. Bitwuzla gives no verdict in any of these configurations. This is also what a hand proof in ESBMC looks like: the hints are assumptions, and the argument that they are true (three small lemmas and congruence) lives outside the program. ESBMC’s --loop-invariant-check applies the invariant rule itself, so the start, the step and the exit no longer need separate programs tied together on paper.

The exit. The 32-bit Gauss loop, which keeps only s and asserts 2 * s == n * (n - 1), broke where we least expected it. With its invariant, both solvers stall on the exit claim: from 2 * s == i * (i - 1), i <= n and !(i < n), conclude 2 * s == n * (n - 1). Written with i == n in place of the two inequalities, the same claim takes 0.46 seconds in both solvers. The solvers never derive the equality and substitute it. They compare two 32-bit multipliers bit by bit, and Lean’s proof avoids that with one line. With __ESBMC_assert(i == n, ...) after the loop and --multi-property, Z3 proves the whole Gauss program in 0.57 seconds. Either change alone leaves it without a verdict.

Two of these moves could become ESBMC heuristics. The exit equality is cheap and local: when an invariant contains i <= n and the loop exits on !(i < n), ESBMC can add i == n and substitute it before checking what follows. Solving the claims of an invariant separately is already an option and could be the default under --loop-invariant-check. The rewriting is harder. As a claim of its own, the identity behind grind’s step, (s + i)2 − (c + i3) = (s2 − c) + i·(2s − i(i − 1)), proves in 0.45 seconds in both solvers, but adding it as a fact to the step does not help. Bitwuzla’s built-in abstraction of multiplication, which by default starts at 33 bits, did not help either when we lowered it to 32 bits on ESBMC’s formulas. What the solvers lack is the use of an equation between products as a rewrite rule. That needs a pass in ESBMC that normalizes polynomials and substitutes the invariant’s equations before the formula reaches the solver. We have not built it; Listing 3 does its job by hand.

Catching a wrong verdict from ESBMC

The other use of a second prover is the one our last post asked for: catching ESBMC when it is wrong. A real test needs a real ESBMC bug, so we took one that ESBMC had until recently (#10537, fixed in #10576) and replayed it on a build from 12 November, before the fix.

The bug involves --ir, which asks ESBMC to treat C integers as mathematical integers that never wrap. --goto2lean follows the same request and uses Lean’s Int, so both routes are asked the same question. ESBMC’s simplifier, the step that precomputes arithmetic on constants before the solver runs, ignored --ir and still wrapped constant results at 32 bits. Here is one of the regression tests from the issue:

int nondet_int(void);
int main() {
  int x = nondet_int();
  __ESBMC_assume(x >= 0 && x <= 10);
  int y = x - 1 - 2147483647;
  __ESBMC_assert(y >= 0, "y >= 0");
  return 0;
}

Under --ir, y is at most −2147483638, so the assertion fails for every x. The old build says VERIFICATION SUCCESSFUL: an unsafe program reported as safe, the error this post began with. Lean’s Int was the right model here. The translation did what --ir asked, and the wrong answer came from ESBMC.

Lean does not accept the translated theorem. Under Int its failure gives no concrete input, though: omega reports only that “a possible counterexample may satisfy the constraints 0 ≤ a ≤ 10”. That range is still enough to settle the question without trusting Lean. We took x = 0 from it and changed the assumption to x == 0. The old build then says VERIFICATION FAILED. A program that is safe for every x between 0 and 10 cannot be unsafe at x = 0, so ESBMC has contradicted itself, and the bug is in ESBMC. Running the old build again with --no-simplify gives FAILED for both versions, which points at the simplifier rather than the SMT encoding or the solver. Current master reports FAILED with x = 0 and y = -2147483648, and Lean proves the negation of the theorem from that witness in four lines:

theorem main_unsafe : ¬ Prog.main (fun _ => True) := by
  intro h
  simp only [Prog.main] at h
  have := (h 0 (by omega)).1
  omega

The same replay does not work on every bug from that issue. In the test y = ~b + INT_MIN, the old build is wrong at b = 0 as well, so fixing a point exposes nothing. --goto2lean also rejects ~ under --ir, so Lean has nothing to say. That is a real gap in the translator, but closing it needs care: the translation has to give ~ the same meaning as ESBMC’s --ir mode, and ESBMC’s own --ir encoding of ~ still wraps at 64 bits (#10596). Until that is settled, rejecting ~ is safer than picking a meaning.

What each answer relies on

We do not trust Lean more than ESBMC across the board. ESBMC writes verification witnesses for violations and proofs, other teams’ validators check them in SV-COMP, and ESBMC can act as a witness validator itself. A validator re-verifies a witness with its own engine, though, so its whole pipeline is trusted in turn. Lean works differently. It is a term that Lean’s kernel checks after the fact, independently of the tactic that built it, so a bug in grind or omega can make a proof fail but cannot make the kernel accept a false theorem (bv_decide is a partial exception, described below the table). The Lean route still relies on other parts, and the table lists them.

Component Shared by both routes? Who checks it
Front end and GOTO conversion Yes Neither route; a front-end bug is invisible to both
Symbolic execution, simplifier, SMT encoding, solver ESBMC only The Lean route, by disagreeing
--goto2lean translator Lean only Trusted; it is not verified
bv_decide proofs Lean only Lean’s kernel, plus compiled code that checks the SAT certificate
omega, grind and hand proofs Lean only Lean’s kernel

#print axioms on a theorem closed by bv_decide lists Lean’s three standard axioms plus axioms named _native.bv_decide: the certificate checker runs as compiled code, so the trusted base includes Lean’s compiler as well as its kernel. Proofs by omega and grind rely on the three standard axioms only.

The check is cheap on these programs. Over the medians of three runs on ten demo programs, translation took about 0.4 seconds for C and C++ and 1.2 seconds for Python (4.4 seconds for the Python program under --ir), and Lean checked each generated file in 1.5 to 1.7 seconds. Most of that is start-up of a Debug build; the numbers say nothing about scalability.

Where each prover is stronger

We ran a handful of small programs through both routes. The verdicts and times are single runs.

Program ESBMC Lean via --goto2lean
Midpoint (lo + hi) / 2, the overflow bug FAILED, lo = hi = 4294967295 bv_decide refutes with the same values
3*x + 5*y != 31 for x, y in 0..10, with --ir FAILED, x = 7, y = 2 omega fails and prints a constraint over its internal bmod_div_term variables; in bit-vector mode bv_decide gives x = 7, y = 2
x * x >= 0, --ir SUCCESSFUL, 0.46 s omega and grind fail; 4-line case split
Gauss sum 2*s == n*(n-1), --ir k-induction UNKNOWN; with the invariant, SUCCESSFUL in 0.47 s same invariant plus grind
Nicomachus, --ir k-induction UNKNOWN; with the invariant, SUCCESSFUL in 0.46 s; a wrong invariant is rejected same invariant plus grind
Nicomachus, 32-bit with the invariant, no verdict in 300 s from Z3 or Bitwuzla; with Listing 3, SUCCESSFUL in 6.0 s (Z3) Listing 2, 4.2 s
Counting loop s == n SUCCESSFUL, invariant synthesized bv_decide with ESBMC’s invariant, 9.5 s
Counting loop with the too-weak invariant s == i UNKNOWN: “loop invariant too weak to prove this claim” refuted, with the state s = i = 4294967295, n = 2147483647
An assertion with __ESBMC_exists SUCCESSFUL, automatic needs a 6-line proof that supplies the witness
Arrays, pointers supported rejected

Which prover wins depends on how the program’s numbers are modeled. With --ir, ESBMC treats integers as mathematical integers that never wrap, and Z3 proved the square, the Gauss sum and Nicomachus in under half a second each; Lean’s integer tactic, omega, handles only linear arithmetic and proves none of them. Over 32-bit words the order reverses: grind proved Nicomachus from the invariant alone, and ESBMC needed Lean’s steps written into the program. Running the 32-bit Nicomachus program with --ir does not move it to the easy side. Under --ir, ESBMC treats unsigned values as unbounded integers that can go negative, so the invariant i <= n fails at entry with a spurious n = 4294967294 (really −2; we reported the misleading trace as #10606). With __ESBMC_assume(n >= 0) added, ESBMC proves the unbounded version in 0.40 seconds, but the 32-bit claim then follows only by a paper argument that ESBMC does not check.

ESBMC finds bugs and prints concrete inputs, handles the whole language, and for simple loops proposes the invariants that Lean needs. Lean asks for more human input, but a proof it accepts is checked by its kernel, and the steps of that proof are instructions ESBMC can follow. The 32-bit Nicomachus loop went from no verdict in either tool to a proof in both, and the ESBMC proof came from reading Lean’s. That exchange is what we want to automate next.

What comes next

  • Heuristics learned from Lean’s proofs. The exit equality and per-claim solving are small changes to ESBMC, and we plan to try them first. The larger one is the rewriting pass that Listing 3 does by hand: normalize polynomials and substitute the invariant’s equations before the formula reaches the solver.
  • Invariants from ESBMC and from models. ESBMC’s synthesis covers loops that grow by a constant. The Nicomachus invariant is the kind of input we ask a language model to propose [2], and when the SMT solvers stall on the step, Lean can still check the proposal.
  • Prove the translator. The translator is the trusted link in the table above. Rafael’s PhD thesis, GOTO: a verification framework for CProver tools (University of Manchester, 2025), gives GOTO a formal semantics, mechanized in part in Isabelle, and treats unwinding, slicing and common-subexpression elimination as transformation passes over it. With that semantics in Lean, we can state the translator’s correctness as a theorem: the weakest precondition that --goto2lean emits implies that no assertion fails in any execution allowed by the semantics. The same semantics lets us state what #10537 broke: a pass must preserve the meaning of the program under the selected encoding.
  • Arrays and pointers. Most of the C code we verify uses them. They need a memory model in Lean that matches ESBMC’s, and memory models are also outside the scope of the thesis’s Isabelle formalization, so this work starts from the same gap.
  • A second route to Lean. ESBMC can write its verification conditions as SMT-LIB 2 files, and LeanWuzla can check bit-vector problems of that kind with bv_decide. We have not yet run it on ESBMC’s output. That route would check the solver’s answer; --goto2lean checks the program.

Join us

We are looking for PhD students, postdocs and collaborators interested in these problems: formal methods, program analysis and interactive theorem proving. ESBMC is open source, and the translator, its regression tests and its documentation are in ESBMC master. If this interests you, email Lucas Cordeiro with a short note on what you would like to work on, or talk to the group first on our public Zulip chat.

References

  • [1] P. V. Dantas, L. C. Cordeiro, and W. S. S. Júnior, “ESBMC: A Survey of Its Evolution, Integration, and Future Directions in Formal Software Verification,” CoRR, vol. abs/2605.26169, 2026, doi: 10.48550/arXiv.2605.26169. DOI
  • [2] M. A. A. Pirzada, G. Reger, A. Bhayat, and L. C. Cordeiro, “LLM-Generated Invariants for Bounded Model Checking Without Loop Unrolling,” in Proceedings of the 39th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering, ASE 2024, Sacramento, CA, USA, October 27 - November 1, 2024, V. Filkov, B. Ray, and M. Zhou, Eds., ACM, 2024, pp. 1395–1407. doi: 10.1145/3691620.3695512. DOI

author.name: Lucas C. Cordeiro and Rafael Sá Menezes

entry.summary: ESBMC can now translate its GOTO programs into Lean 4. We ran both provers on the same programs to see where each one is stronger, what ESBMC can learn from Lean's proofs, and what a disagreement between them tells us.

entry.title: LLMs propose, verifiers check: our work on LLMs and formal verification

link.title: LLMs propose, verifiers check: our work on LLMs and formal verification

entry.content:
A language model can produce a loop invariant, a function contract or a patch in seconds. It cannot tell you whether any of those things is actually correct. A model checker can. Unwinding assertions confirm that a loop bound covers every iteration, k-induction proves properties of unbounded executions, and ranking functions prove that loops terminate. The checker still needs a property to verify, and for deep/nested loops and large codebases the proof often depends on an invariant or contract that no one has written. Each side fills a gap in the other.

Since 2023 our Systems and Software Security (S3) group at the University of Manchester and our collaborators have looked at what happens when the two share a loop. Much of this work has used ESBMC, the SMT-based model checker that we develop. ESBMC combines abstract interpretation through interval analysis, model checking through bounded model checking and k-induction, deductive verification through function contracts [1], and SMT solving. A recent survey looks at how it has become the verification backend for LLM-based tools [2].

flowchart LR
    T["Task<br/>program, property,<br/>or requirement"] --> L["LLM proposes<br/>code, patch, invariant,<br/>contract, spec, translation"]
    L --> V{"Formal tool checks<br/>ESBMC,<br/>automated theorem prover"}
    V -- "holds" --> A["Accepted artifact<br/>with a proof or<br/>bounded guarantee"]
    V -- "fails" --> C["Counterexample<br/>trace, line, property"]
    C --> L

Figure 1. The loop shared by most of the papers below. The LLM never makes the correctness decision; the formal tool does.

Our work since 2023

1. How safe is LLM-generated code?

We started off by asking how often LLM-written code is unsafe, and used ESBMC to find out. More than half of the C programs that GPT-3.5-turbo wrote for our FormAI dataset had at least one vulnerability [3], and a follow-up across nine LLMs found at least 62% [4].

Model checking every completion is too slow for an IDE, so we used these verifier-checked labels to train SecureFalcon, a small classifier that flags vulnerable code instantly on a CPU [5].

Formal tools have blind spots too. On the CASTLE benchmark, ESBMC raised the fewest false alarms but missed vulnerabilities outside the properties it checks, such as weak cryptography, while LLMs got worse as programs grew [6]. A survey chapter covers the wider area [7].

2. Counterexample-guided repair and generation

When ESBMC finds a violation, it returns a counterexample: a concrete input and the execution trace that leads to the failing check. That makes it a precise bug report, so we pass it back to an LLM. ESBMC-AI (posted May 2023) takes the source code, the counterexample and the stack trace and feeds it to an LLM, and ESBMC then re-verifies the patch. It was evaluated on 50k FormAI programs [8]. ESBMC-AI has since been succeeded by Entoli, an open-source agent with formal-verification-based workflows. The same loop also works for neural-network code: ESBMC checked about 81k mutated neural-network programs, and an LLM repaired the bugs that ESBMC found [9]. VeriExploit runs it in reverse: you start with a Solidity counterexample and an LLM generates an attacker contract which re-triggers the bug. That contract is then validated by a model checker and is able to reproduce 85.60% of the bugs in our benchmark [10]. For legacy C code, UnitTenX turns ESBMC counterexamples into readable unit tests [11].

3. LLMs supply what the verifier is missing

Here the LLM writes out the invariants and contracts that a proof needs, and a sound tool then decides whether to believe them.

  • Invariants. ESBMC ibmc replaces each loop with an LLM-generated invariant which a theorem prover then checks. It was able to verify programs that SeaHorn and VeriAbs were unable to verify and went on to receive an ACM SIGSOFT Distinguished Paper Award [12]. VerIbmc takes the same approach using open-weight models on a single local machine and solves 431 of the 499 problems in its best configuration, GPT-OSS-120B [13].
  • Contracts. ConVer takes a top-level property and synthesizes function contracts from it, refining them in a CEGAR-CEGIS loop and achieving 82-96% success on 45 Frama-C programs, the easiest of its four benchmark suites, and as low as 33% on the harder ones [14]. For regression verification, partial LLM-inferred contracts produced zero false equivalence proofs on EqBench-C [15].
  • Agents. Agentic model checking is based on the principle of ‘agents propose, solvers verify’ where the agent works out the specifications and plans the run, with all soundness-critical decisions remaining with the bounded model checker (CBMC and Kani). On mature, heavily fuzzed software it found 68 source-audited defects across 11 projects [16].

4. From prose and other languages to checkable models

SpecVerify uses Claude 3.5 Sonnet in conjunction with ESBMC to derive properties from requirements. On nine of Lockheed Martin’s cyber-physical systems it achieved the same result as NASA’s CoCoSim but with fewer false positives [17]. The models still occasionally misread the specifications, so human review remained necessary. INVAR takes a document (e.g. the USB 2.0 or CXL 4.0 specification) and extracts a transition system from it, which it then checks with NuSMV and reports any missing evidence as a named gap rather than a vacuous pass [18]. With NASA JPL we use an LLM to translate Python into C for ESBMC. The paper makes the caveat that as the translation doesn’t prove equivalence the outcome is only bug finding and not verification [19]; the agent and benchmark are both public.

5. Reviews of the field

Two reviews place this work in a wider context: one which provides a taxonomy of the generative transformations and their recurring patterns in over 100 LLM-based proposals for software verification and falsification [20], and one which is a systematic review of 38 studies on LLM agents, which identifies specification as the bottleneck rather than checking [21].

How the pieces fit together

timeline
    2023 : FormAI dataset
         : ESBMC-AI preprint
    2024 : LLM invariants, ESBMC ibmc
         : Repair of neural-network code
    2025 : FormAI-v2, nine LLMs
         : SecureFalcon, CASTLE
         : SpecVerify, VeriExploit, UnitTenX
    2026 : ConVer, VerIbmc, partial contracts
         : Python translation, INVAR
    2027 : Agentic model checking

Figure 2. Timeline by publication year, or by first preprint for ESBMC-AI and for work not yet at a venue.

The papers all follow the same pattern of division of labor. The LLM does the semantic guessing (what a loop maintains, what a function assumes, what a requirement means). A sound tool provides the guarantee. Over time the LLM has been trusted to do more and more. It started off just being measured, then it was used to repair code under a whole-program verifier, then it was used to write parts of the proof and in the agentic model checking work it’s used to plan the entire run. Invariants and contracts are proved before they are used, so a wrong guess is rejected. Assumptions about the environment are different: they are trusted, not checked. If an LLM writes an assumption that rules out every input reaching an assertion, the verifier reports success vacuously. That is why our pipelines check the evidence itself: each LLM-written harness has a seeded-bug twin that must fail, and INVAR reports missing evidence as a gap rather than a pass. A number of the papers are also direct extensions of one another. FormAI provided the evaluation set for ESBMC-AI and the training data for SecureFalcon. VerIbmc builds on the ibmc invariant work.

The negative results are just as important as the positive ones. CASTLE shows us the limitations of the formal tools. SpecVerify shows that the prose still requires a human to read it. The Python work is very clear that, without a verified translation, the method can find bugs but cannot prove the code correct.

Lessons learned

Benchmarks come with an answer key; production code does not. In recent work an LLM agent drafted verification harnesses for codebases such as the AWS SDK for C++, NVIDIA OpenSMA firmware and vLLM, ESBMC checked them, and maintainers merged 18 fixes upstream, including fixes for two CVEs in the AWS SDK for C++. Five lessons from that work and the papers above, presented at FATTW 2026:

  1. Zero false positives beats a higher proof rate. Developers stop trusting a tool that raises false alarms.
  2. Maintainers fix what arrives with a concrete input. The counterexample is the bug report.
  3. The generator’s quality still propagates. With GPT-4o instead of Claude 3.5 Sonnet, SpecVerify produced 8 false positives instead of 0.
  4. We do not win every benchmark. SeaHorn proves more programs than ibmc, and CoCoSim matches SpecVerify; portfolios beat single tools.
  5. Verifiers have traps too. Zero verification conditions, disabled unwinding assertions and contracts that silently check nothing all look like success, so the evidence itself needs checking.

What comes next

There are three challenges that neither academia nor industry can solve alone:

  • Verification at generation speed. Agents generate code in seconds, while industrial proofs take minutes to hours. Faster tools will not close this gap entirely: program verification is undecidable in general (Rice’s theorem), so some checks can end in a timeout or an unknown verdict. Checking must reuse earlier proofs incrementally and report honestly when it cannot decide.
  • Guarantees for agent workflows. Verifying each agent is not enough to verify the workflow they form; we need compositional contracts between agents.
  • Evidence we can trust. DO-178C, the standard for airborne software, already accepts formal evidence through its formal methods supplement, DO-333, which raises the question of who checks the checker. Witnesses and validators are part of the answer.

Underneath all three sits the problem that every line of work above runs into: how do we validate a specification an LLM has derived from natural language before anything is proved against it?

Join us

We’re looking for PhD students, postdocs and collaborators who are interested in working on these problems (formal methods, program analysis, machine learning etc). Our tools are open source and most of the papers listed above come with the associated artifacts so you can run them. If this is of interest to you then just get in touch with Lucas Cordeiro with a brief note on what you’d like to work on. To talk with the group first, join our public Zulip chat.

entry.title: Google Gemini updates: Flash 1.5, Gemma 2 and Project Astra

link.title: Google Gemini updates: Flash 1.5, Gemma 2 and Project Astra

entry.content:
Gemini breaks new ground with a faster model, longer context, AI agents and moreLearn more:Learn more:Learn more:Models & ResearchProductsInfrastructure & cloudTechnology Learn more: ProductsPlatformsDevices Learn more: Outreach & initiativesLeadershipInside Google Learn more: May 14, 2024 We’re introducing a series of updates across the Gemini family of models, including the new 1.5 Flash, our lightweight model for speed and efficiency, and Project Astra, our vision for the future of AI assistants. Demis HassabisCEO of Google DeepMind, on behalf of the Gemini teamIn December, we launched our first natively multimodal model Gemini 1.0 in three sizes: Ultra, Pro and Nano. Just a few months later we released 1.5 Pro, with enhanced performance and a breakthrough long context window of 1 million tokens.Developers and enterprise customers have been putting 1.5 Pro to use in incredible ways and finding its long context window, multimodal reasoning capabilities and impressive overall performance incredibly useful.We know from user feedback that some applications need lower latency and a lower cost to serve. This inspired us to keep innovating, so today, we’re introducing Gemini 1.5 Flash: a model that’s lighter-weight than 1.5 Pro, and designed to be fast and efficient to serve at scale.Both 1.5 Pro and 1.5 Flash are available in public preview with a 1 million token context window in Google AI Studio and Vertex AI. And now, 1.5 Pro is also available with a 2 million token context window via waitlist to developers using the API and to Google Cloud customers.We’re also introducing updates across the Gemini family of models, announcing our next generation of open models, Gemma 2, and sharing progress on the future of AI assistants, with Project Astra.Context lengths of leading foundation models compared with Gemini 1.5’s 2 million token capability1.5 Flash is the newest addition to the Gemini model family and the fastest Gemini model served in the API. It’s optimized for high-volume, high-frequency tasks at scale, is more cost-efficient to serve and features our breakthrough long context window.While it’s a lighter weight model than 1.5 Pro, it’s highly capable of multimodal reasoning across vast amounts of information and delivers impressive quality for its size.The new Gemini 1.5 Flash model is optimized for speed and efficiency, is highly capable of multimodal reasoning and features our breakthrough long context window.1.5 Flash excels at summarization, chat applications, image and video captioning, data extraction from long documents and tables, and more. This is because it’s been trained by 1.5 Pro through a process called “distillation,” where the most essential knowledge and skills from a larger model are transferred to a smaller, more efficient model.Read more about 1.5 Flash in our updated Gemini 1.5 technical report, on the Gemini technology page, and learn about 1.5 Flash’s availability and pricing.Over the last few months, we’ve significantly improved 1.5 Pro, our best model for general performance across a wide range of tasks.Beyond extending its context window to 2 million tokens, we’ve enhanced its code generation, logical reasoning and planning, multi-turn conversation, and audio and image understanding through data and algorithmic advances. We see strong improvements on public and internal benchmarks for each of these tasks.1.5 Pro can now follow increasingly complex and nuanced instructions, including ones that specify product-level behavior involving role, format and style. We’ve improved control over the model’s responses for specific use cases, like crafting the persona and response style of a chat agent or automating workflows through multiple function calls. And we’ve enabled users to steer model behavior by setting system instructions.We added audio understanding in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio, so 1.5 Pro can now reason across image and audio for videos uploaded in Google AI Studio. And we’re now integrating 1.5 Pro into Google products, including Gemini Advanced and in Workspace apps.Read more about 1.5 Pro in our updated Gemini 1.5 technical report and on the Gemini technology page.Gemini Nano is expanding beyond text-only inputs to include images as well. Starting with Pixel, applications using Gemini Nano with Multimodality will be able to understand the world the way people do — not just through text, but also through sight, sound and spoken language.Read more about Gemini 1.0 Nano on Android.Today, we’re also sharing a series of updates to Gemma, our family of open models built from the same research and technology used to create the Gemini models.We’re announcing Gemma 2, our next generation of open models for responsible AI innovation. Gemma 2 has a new architecture designed for breakthrough performance and efficiency, and will be available in new sizes.The Gemma family is also expanding with PaliGemma, our first vision-language model inspired by PaLI-3. And we’ve upgraded our Responsible Generative AI Toolkit with LLM Comparator for evaluating the quality of model responses.Read more on the Developer blog.As part of Google DeepMind’s mission to build AI responsibly to benefit humanity, we’ve always wanted to develop universal AI agents that can be helpful in everyday life. That’s why today, we’re sharing our progress in building the future of AI assistants with Project Astra (advanced seeing and talking responsive agent).To be truly useful, an agent needs to understand and respond to the complex and dynamic world just like people do — and take in and remember what it sees and hears to understand context and take action. It also needs to be proactive, teachable and personal, so users can talk to it naturally and without lag or delay.While we’ve made incredible progress developing AI systems that can understand multimodal information, getting response time down to something conversational is a difficult engineering challenge. Over the past few years, we’ve been working to improve how our models perceive, reason and converse to make the pace and quality of interaction feel more natural.Building on Gemini, we’ve developed prototype agents that can process information faster by continuously encoding video frames, combining the video and speech input into a timeline of events, and caching this information for efficient recall.By leveraging our leading speech models, we also enhanced how they sound, giving the agents a wider range of intonations. These agents can better understand the context they’re being used in, and respond quickly, in conversation.With technology like this, it’s easy to envision a future where people could have an expert AI assistant by their side, through a phone or glasses. And some of these capabilities are coming to Google products, like the Gemini app and web experience, later this year.We’ve made incredible progress so far with our family of Gemini models, and we’re always striving to advance the state-of-the-art even further. By investing in a relentless production line of innovation, we’re able to explore new ideas at the frontier, while also unlocking the possibility of new and exciting Gemini use cases.Learn more about Gemini and its capabilities.Collection Sign up for our newsletters with product updates, event information, special offers, and more.
